title: Natural law (CCC 1954–1960)
hook: a moral sense written in human reason, shared across cultures

segments.voice: Yesterday, subsidiarity: the larger community helps, and doesn't take over. Your line was closest hands first. Whom did you let do something their own way? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

Two small children at a playground, on holiday, from two different countries. They share no language at all. They've been taking turns on the slide, and it's working. Then one of them cuts in front. The other one doesn't need a single word. Hands on hips, a frown, a finger pointing back at the line. Everybody watching understands it at once: that's not fair. Nobody taught them the same rulebook. They didn't grow up in the same religion, or any religion. And still something in each of them recognized the same wrong. Paul noticed something like this, writing to the Christians in Rome. The Catechism builds a whole teaching on it.
screen: `NO SHARED LANGUAGE.` → `ONE CUTS THE LINE.` → `THAT'S NOT FAIR.`

segments.voice: The phrase is natural law. Not the laws of nature, like gravity. A moral law. The Catechism says it expresses the original moral sense that lets a person tell, by reason, good from evil, and truth from a lie. It quotes Saint Thomas Aquinas: the natural law is the light of understanding placed in us by God, by which we know what we must do and what we must avoid. God gave this light, Thomas says, at creation. Why natural? Not because animals follow it, the Catechism says, but because reason, which declares it, belongs to human nature. Then Paul. Writing about people who never received the law of Moses, he says that when they do by nature what the law asks, they show, in the Douay-Rheims, "the work of the law written in their hearts." That's the sense of today's line. The Catechism says the natural law is present in the heart of each person, and it quotes the Roman writer Cicero: there is a true law, right reason, in agreement with nature, spread among all people. And yet, it says, how the law is applied varies, and takes reflection, in different places, times and circumstances. It also says the law is unchanging through history, and that even when it's denied, it can't be destroyed or erased from the human heart. It always rises again. Last, an honest limit. The Catechism admits that the precepts of natural law aren't seen by everyone clearly and at once. That's why, it says, people need grace and revelation too, so moral truth can be known easily, firmly and without error. Tomorrow picks up that word, grace.
screen: `NOT GRAVITY: A MORAL SENSE.` · `A LIGHT OF UNDERSTANDING FROM GOD.` · `WRITTEN IN THEIR HEARTS.` · `NOT ALWAYS SEEN CLEARLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a moral truth everyone knows. Settle, and breathe. Think of a few things you've seen people react to in the same way, across ages and backgrounds. Someone cheated. A promise broken. A child treated cruelly. A stranger who stopped to help. Pick one, and stay with it. Notice whether you had to look it up. Notice whether it shows up anywhere in the body, or nowhere at all. If you pray, you can give thanks for that light. If you don't, just let it be there, quietly, a moment longer. The bell holds the time.
Natural law. The moral sense written in human reason, by which people tell good from evil: in the Catechism's words, a light of understanding placed in us by God. Today's word.
Your line: written in reason. Today, when you find yourself agreeing with someone very different from you about right and wrong, stop and notice it. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching appeals to natural law when speaking with people of every faith or none, arguing from reason as well as from scripture.

fork.setup: a friend says, "if people don't share my religion, we have nothing to say to each other about right and wrong." what does the Catechism's natural law teaching suggest?
options: that's right; morality is only for believers.
there's common ground written in human reason.
everyone's sense of right and wrong is just personal taste.
fork.reveal: the Catechism says the natural law is present in every heart and shared through reason, even as its application varies.
